thesis: Whether cognitive processes and learning-related behaviors established in laboratory category-learning research transfer to immersive VR is tested by comparing IVR (HTC Vive), desktop-3D, and 2D eye-tracked versions of an identical four-category classification task, framed through an information-access-cost lens (predicted ordering 2D < desktop-3D < VR); the central finding is that learning accuracy is statistically equivalent across all three media despite real differences in response time, fixation behavior, and attentional-optimization trajectory, which the authors read as license to presume desktop-based findings and design principles transfer to VR contexts without medium-specific re-validation, subject to individual-differences and VR-attrition caveats.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Frames VR as both a methodological opportunity (controlled presentation of novel stimuli) and an open empirical question for cognitive science; argues category learning is well suited to cross-medium comparison because it taps information access, attention, and learning simultaneously.

sections.title: Same tasks, different experiences
sections.summary: Surveys VR-specific physical/perceptual differences (near-eye fixed screen distance, decoupled accommodation/convergence, restricted field of view, motion-tracked controllers) and the presence/engagement literature; cites Makransky's findings that immersive VR raises cognitive load and often reduces learning outcomes unless paired with generative-learning, enactment, or pre-training techniques; introduces the desirable-difficulty vs added-cognitive-load debate over VR's motor interaction costs.

sections.title: New interface, same cognitive processes
sections.summary: Reviews VR-desktop equivalence evidence: Hamilton et al.'s review (10/29 studies show no VR-vs-desktop difference), Angel-Urdinola et al.'s meta-analysis (more than half neutral-positive), Parong & Mayer's 2D-slides-initially-outperform-VR finding with reflection-prompt catch-up; VR-based cognitive-test validity work (Stroop, Posner, memory).

sections.title: Category learning
sections.summary: Introduces the category-learning paradigm and information-access-cost literature (Meier & Blair; Rajsic et al.; Morgan et al.), motivating the prediction that higher access cost (VR > desktop-3D > 2D) should accelerate attentional optimization.

sections.title: Methods
sections.summary: 179 SFU undergraduates randomized to VR (HTC Vive HMD + hand controllers, n=58), desktop-3D (22-inch screen + gamepad, n=56), or 2D eye-tracked (Tobii X120 + gamepad, n=65); 4-category, 3-feature (2 relevant, 1 irrelevant) classification task run to a 24-consecutive-correct criterion or 240 trials/30 minutes.

sections.title: Exclusions
sections.summary: 32 VR non-learners excluded (6 of whom withdrew citing physical discomfort), 30 3D non-learners excluded; 2D group lost most participants to dropout/equipment failure, leaving only 8 of 65 with complete criterion-meeting datasets; missingness checked against a prior study and treated as at-random.

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: No condition differences in accuracy; 2D significantly faster response times, shorter fixation durations; VR highest fixation counts throughout; attentional optimization shows a bin-by-condition interaction with 2D exceeding VR/3D optimization by experiment's end; feedback-viewing duration shows no condition effect.

sections.title: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.summary: Argues strong cross-medium equivalence in learning-accuracy trajectories supports transferring desktop-based cognitive/pedagogical findings to VR contexts; the predicted monotonic access-cost ordering held for only one measure (fixation count, wrong direction), attributed to novelty/enjoyment rather than cost; flags VR-specific attrition (motion sickness, fatigue, dizziness) as a practical cost against any VR benefit; notes individual differences (spatial ability) as an unmeasured likely moderator.

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: operationalized architecturally as the condition ladder itself (VR high / desktop-3D medium / 2D low access-cost), not measured via a separate presence instrument; presence definition cited from the lit review but not administered

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: invoked in the lit review via Makransky's finding that immersive VR often raises cognitive load; treated as a candidate explanatory mechanism, not measured directly in this study

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: VR/desktop-3D require active motor manipulation (hand-controller collision / gamepad D-pad) to reveal features one at a time; 2D presents all features simultaneously to a passive, eye-tracked viewer

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: central DV: accuracy (criterion-restricted) and response time jointly index category-learning skill acquisition; equivalent trajectories found across all three media

constructs.label: cybersickness & physical discomfort
constructs.treatment: VR-specific attrition: 6/32 VR non-learner exclusions withdrew citing physical discomfort (motion sickness, dizziness, fatigue, headache); one 2D dropout citing dizziness

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: post-hoc, unmeasured explanation for VR's elevated fixation count: novelty of arm-controller manipulation framed as intrinsically pleasing

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: not operationalized; gestured toward via citations (Jensen & Konradsen; Farra, Smith & Ulrich) suggesting VR enthusiasm may be a single-session novelty effect

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: held constant as a design control: cube geometry, category structure, and feature location/relevance combinations matched across VR/desktop-3D; 2D uses a flat triangular analogue of the same structure

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.apparatus: HTC Vive headset + HTC Vive hand controllers; open testing area, standing; features revealed by physically colliding a hand controller with the stimulus cube to rotate it; category selected by reaching to an on-screen button and pulling the trigger
conditions.task: 4-category, 3-feature (2 relevant, 1 irrelevant) classification task, 240 trials or 30 minutes, 24-consecutive-correct criterion
conditions.exclusions: 32 non-learners excluded; 6 of these withdrew citing physical discomfort
conditions.effectDirection: No accuracy difference vs 3D/2D; response time and fixation duration similar to 3D (both slower/longer than 2D); highest fixation count of all conditions, not converging to 3D/2D's lower asymptote

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.apparatus: standard Windows 10 desktop, 22-inch color monitor, Logitech F310 gamepad; identical stimulus cube rotated via gamepad D-pad; category selected via bumpers/triggers
conditions.effectDirection: No accuracy difference vs VR/2D; response time and fixation duration statistically indistinguishable from VR; fixation count starts higher than 2D but converges to 2D's lower asymptote by experiment's end

conditions.label: 2D video / slideshow / text
conditions.apparatus: same 22-inch monitor + gamepad (category response only); flat triangular stimulus with all three features simultaneously visible; Tobii X120 eye tracker, 60Hz sampling, 0.5° spatial resolution, 60cm viewing distance, 75ms temporal / 1.9° spatial fixation thresholds, per-participant calibration
conditions.task: identical category structure to VR/3D, presented as a flat triangular analogue
conditions.exclusions: 1 dropout citing dizziness; equipment failure left only 8 of the remaining participants with complete criterion-meeting gaze datasets; missingness checked against a prior study with the same structure and treated as at-random
conditions.effectDirection: No accuracy difference vs VR/3D; significantly faster response times and shorter, flatter fixation durations than VR/3D; lower initial attentional optimization but exceeds VR/3D optimization by experiment's end

readings.claim: Learning accuracy trajectories are statistically equivalent across IVR, desktop-3D, and 2D conditions of an identical category-learning task.
Only the 2D condition differs on response time; VR and desktop-3D response times do not differ from each other.
The predicted access-cost ordering (2D < 3D < VR) held for only one of six measures — fixation count — and in the opposite of the predicted direction; the manipulation is judged largely ineffective.
VR's elevated, non-converging fixation count is more plausibly explained by novelty/enjoyment of the arm-controller interaction than by access cost per se.

Because general learning-outcome and information-access patterns replicate across VR, desktop-3D, and 2D, desktop-based cognitive/pedagogical findings and design principles should be presumed to transfer to VR without medium-specific re-validation.
Individual differences such as spatial ability likely moderate any VR-specific learning benefit or cost that a between-subjects average would mask.
VR-specific attrition from physical discomfort (motion sickness, dizziness, fatigue, headache) is a real practical cost to be weighed against any VR learning benefit.

concepts.term: category-learning cube stimulus (4 categories, 3 binary features)

interlocutors.name: Makransky, Guido
interlocutors.role: cited for the recurring finding that immersive VR groups show higher cognitive load than other instruction, sometimes offset by generative-learning/enactment/pre-training pairings

interlocutors.name: Parong, Jocelyn & Mayer, Richard
interlocutors.role: cited for 2D slide-based learning initially outperforming a 12-minute VR biology lesson, with VR catching up once reflection prompts were added

interlocutors.name: Hamilton, D. et al. (VR-education review)
interlocutors.role: 29-study review: 10 showed no VR-vs-desktop learning-outcome difference, 2 showed worse VR outcomes

interlocutors.name: Angel-Urdinola, D. et al. (VR meta-analysis)
interlocutors.role: meta-analysis reporting an overall positive but more-than-half neutral-positive effect of VR on learning outcomes

interlocutors.name: Zhao, J. et al. (VR spatial memory)
interlocutors.role: found no VR advantage over desktop simulation for landmark memory; some advantages favored desktop

interlocutors.name: Meier, M. & Blair, M. (information-access cost)
interlocutors.role: prior lab manipulation of information-access cost (3-second reveal delay) motivating this study's cost framing

interlocutors.name: Rajsic, J. et al. (information-access cost)
interlocutors.role: four-experiment demonstration that increasing access costs, including added motor cost, accelerates adoption of optimal information-access patterns

interlocutors.name: Wood, S. et al. (information-access cost)
interlocutors.role: contrasted in Discussion: used fixed, obtrusive delays vs this study's self-paced motor delays, offered as an explanation for the largely-ineffective cost manipulation here

interlocutors.name: McColeman, C. et al. (information-access behaviors)
interlocutors.role: cited for medium-agnostic information-access patterns (eye-movements vs mouse/keyboard; category learning vs StarCraft 2)

interlocutors.name: Sun, R., Wu, Y. J. & Cai, Q. (spatial ability x VR)
interlocutors.role: individual-differences moderation: low-spatial-ability learners benefit most from VR, high-spatial-ability learners no better than paper-based learning

tensions.axis: media-comparison equivalence (this paper's accuracy null) vs immersion-optimism (Strand B affordance literature)
tensions.note: This paper's central null accuracy result sits on the equivalence pole of debate axis 5 (desktop-3D as sufficient proxy for IVR) named in the cluster plan; it directly qualifies affordance-optimist readings elsewhere in Strand B by showing no learning-accuracy advantage for either 3D or IVR over 2D.

The study's own predicted cost ordering mostly failed to materialize, leaving the desirable-difficulty vs cognitive-load framing from the Introduction largely untested rather than resolved by the Results.

tensions.axis: VR engagement as durable benefit vs VR engagement as single-session novelty artifact
tensions.note: The paper's own speculative reading of elevated VR fixation counts leaves open whether repeated exposure would erode the effect; not tested within this design.
